query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting the fixed EAM reference with an adaptive, actively learned neural network interatomic potential (NNIP) that is trained on ab initio configurations of both the solid and liquid phases of multicomponent high-entropy alloys near their melting temperatures will improve the phase‐space overlap between the reference and target systems.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys in equilibrium at high melting temperatures, existing in both solid and liquid states.
generation.intervention: Implement an active-learning on‐the‐fly training scheme to develop a neural network potential that incorporates representative ab initio liquid configurations, and use this NNIP as the reference during thermodynamic integration.
generation.conditions: Applied to equimolar or near-equimolar high-entropy alloys (e.g., quinary or higher systems) in temperature regimes close to their melting points (within roughly ±10% of Tm), where solid and liquid configurations coexist or are accessible.
generation.structural_mediator: The NNIP, with its flexible functional form, better captures the broad spectrum of atomic configurations (including disordered liquid-like states) compared to EAM potentials.
generation.mechanism: By training on a diverse set of ab initio configurations including high-temperature liquid states, the NNIP produces a smoother, more continuous free-energy landscape that reduces the integration path mismatch. This enhanced reference–target overlap leads to a more accurate and efficient thermodynamic integration than that achieved with conventional EAM-based TOR-TILD references.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable reduction in the thermodynamic-integration path mismatch, with an anticipated reduction on the order of 30–50% relative to TOR-TILD’s current EAM references, resulting in free energy estimates that are closer (e.g., within ~5 meV/atom) to full ab initio molecular dynamics benchmarks.
generation.baseline: The current TOR-TILD approach using EAM potentials, which exhibits significant mismatches in the integration pathway due to its limited configurational flexibility for representing ab initio liquid states.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be most effective for high-entropy alloys with complex, multicomponent chemistries near their melting points; its utility for simpler systems or significantly undercooled liquids is uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The exact percentage reduction in integration path mismatch and the quantitative free-energy accuracy gain remain uncertain until benchmarked across a representative set of alloy compositions and temperature conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform thermodynamic integration calculations for a set of representative multicomponent high-entropy alloys near their melting temperatures using both the standard EAM-based TOR-TILD method and the new active-learning NNIP-based reference. Compare the computed free energies with fully converged ab initio molecular dynamics free-energy assessments.
measurements: The thermodynamic integration path mismatch (quantified as the deviation along the integration pathway) for both methods.
The absolute free-energy difference (in meV/atom) between the method under test and the ab initio benchmark.
Statistical measures of convergence and reproducibility across multiple alloy compositions and temperature points.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the NNIP-based method does not yield a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than 30% reduction in the integration path mismatch or free energy accuracy not improved to within ~5 meV/atom of the benchmark) relative to the EAM-based method, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
A map of single-phase high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys have exhibited unusual materials properties. The stability of equimolar single-phase solid solution of five or more elements is supposedly rare and identifying the existence of such alloys has been challenging because of the vast chemical space of possible combinations. Herein, based on high-throughput density-functional theory calculations, we construct a chemical map of single-phase equimolar high-entropy alloys by investigating over 658,000 equimolar quinary alloys through a binary regular solid-solution model. We identify 30,201 potential single-phase equimolar alloys (5% of the possible combinations) forming mainly in body-centered cubic structures. We unveil the chemistries that are likely to form high-entropy alloys, and identify the complex interplay among mixing enthalpy, intermetallics formation, and melting point that drives the formation of these solid solutions. We demonstrate the power of our method by predicting the existence of two new high-entropy alloys, i.e. the body-centered cubic AlCoMnNiV and the face-centered cubic CoFeMnNiZn, which are successfully synthesized.Subject terms: Mat
